idiom_name: System.Threading.Channels bounded channel + Task readers (single-reader dispatch or fan-out)
implementation_notes: The classic dispatcher collapses into System.Threading.Channels: Channel.CreateBounded<T> is the queue, ChannelReader.ReadAllAsync() is the consumer loop, and a Task.Run(async () => await foreach ...) per reader is a performer - with SingleReader/SingleWriter promising the access pattern so the implementation can drop locks. A single-reader dispatcher plus an ActionBlock (or a semaphore) is the form to choose when the selection must be central; the bounded channel's FullMode supplies back-pressure (Wait) or explicit loss (DropOldest/DropWrite). Use Channel.CreateUnbounded only when the producer is genuinely rate-limited by something else; Task/PLINQ remain the simpler tools when the performers are equivalent and uncoordinated.
pitfalls: A channel is never finished by itself: without Writer.Complete() (or cancellation) ReadAllAsync() awaits forever and the performers never exit.
A reader loop whose handler throws kills that Task; unless the exception is observed (await/log) the performer silently disappears and the remaining readers absorb the load.

CreateUnbounded is the default in many samples but gives no back-pressure at all: overload becomes heap growth, and BoundedChannelFullMode.DropWrite/DropOldest silently discards messages unless an itemDropped callback is registered.
Declaring SingleReader = true while starting several readers is a correctness bug hidden by the option: the channel may skip synchronization the readers rely on.

variants.name: TPL Dataflow ActionBlock with MaxDegreeOfParallelism
variants.implementation_notes: TPL Dataflow compiles the dispatcher and the performer pool into one declarative block: an ActionBlock<TInput> has an internal queue, invokes the configured delegate for every posted element and runs at most MaxDegreeOfParallelism of them at a time, so post() is the dispatch and the delegate is the performer. Complete() then Completion await drains it. It is the right form for multi-stage flows (the block links into a pipeline) and when the degree of parallelism is configuration; it is heavier than a channel when messages are simply fanned out, and the Dataflow assembly ships as a NuGet package rather than in the shared framework.
pitfalls: ActionBlock.Post() returns false and silently drops the message when BoundedCapacity is reached; use SendAsync (which awaits) or inspect the return value.
Exceptions from the delegate fault the whole block permanently: it stops accepting input and every subsequent Post/SendAsync fails until the block is replaced.
OutputCount/InputCount and Completion are the only observability hooks; without them a stalled block is indistinguishable from a slow one.
MaxDegreeOfParallelism = -1 (unbounded) plus BoundedCapacity = -1 gives no limits at all, which is the overload failure mode the pattern exists to avoid.
